questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On a topographical map, the scale expressed as '1 centimetre represents 1 kilometre' is an example of a
questions.explanation: A statement scale expresses the map-to-ground relationship in words, unlike a representative fraction which uses a ratio.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A scale expressed as a ratio, such as 1:50,000, with no units attached, is called a
questions.explanation: A representative fraction shows the ratio between map distance and ground distance, applicable regardless of the unit of measurement used.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A scale drawn as a line divided into units to allow direct measurement of distances on a map is called a
questions.explanation: A linear scale is a drawn bar marked with distance units, allowing map users to measure ground distances directly using a ruler or divider.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: If a map has a scale of 1:50,000, a distance of 4 centimetres on the map represents an actual ground distance of
questions.explanation: 4 cm x 50,000 = 200,000 cm = 2,000 metres = 2 kilometres on the ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The direction of a point on a map, measured clockwise from north and expressed in degrees, is called its
questions.explanation: Bearing gives the precise direction to a point, measured in degrees clockwise from north (0°/360°).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The imaginary lines on a topographical map joining points of equal height above sea level are called
questions.explanation: Contour lines represent equal elevation, allowing the shape and steepness of the land to be visualised on a flat map.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Where contour lines are drawn very close together on a map, the land they represent is
questions.explanation: Closely spaced contour lines indicate rapid changes in elevation over a short horizontal distance, representing steep slopes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Where contour lines are widely spaced apart on a map, the land they represent is
questions.explanation: Widely spaced contours indicate a gradual change in elevation, representing gently sloping terrain.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A steep, near-vertical rock face, often found at a coastline or valley edge, is best identified on a map by
options: concentric circles far apart from each other
the complete absence of contour lines
widely spaced, evenly distributed contour lines
closely packed contour lines forming a near-continuous line
questions.explanation: A cliff is shown where contour lines converge tightly, sometimes merging, indicating an almost vertical change in elevation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A long, narrow depression, usually containing a river, and bounded by higher land on either side, is called a
questions.explanation: A valley is a low-lying stretch of land between hills or mountains, typically formed by river erosion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A narrow strip of high land projecting outward from a mountain or hill, often between two valleys, is called a
questions.explanation: A spur is a projecting ridge of higher ground extending from a main upland area, often separating two valleys.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: An extensive area of flat or gently undulating low-lying land is called a
questions.explanation: A plain is a large area of relatively flat land at low elevation, often suited to agriculture and settlement.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: An extensive, relatively flat area of land raised significantly above sea level, often with steep sides, is called a
questions.explanation: A plateau is an elevated flatland, distinguished from a plain mainly by its higher elevation and often steep-sided edges.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A diagram showing the shape of the land surface along a straight line drawn across a map is called a
questions.explanation: A cross-section is constructed by plotting the elevations along a chosen line to reveal the profile of the terrain.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On a topographical map, settlements that cluster closely together around a central point, such as a market or road junction, are described as having a
questions.explanation: Nucleated settlements are tightly clustered around a focal point, unlike dispersed settlements which are spread out.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The shape and size of the Earth is best described as
options: a perfect sphere with no flattening
questions.explanation: The Earth bulges slightly at the equator and is flattened at the poles due to its rotation, making it an oblate spheroid rather than a perfect sphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The spinning of the Earth on its own axis, completing one full turn approximately every 24 hours, is called
questions.explanation: Rotation is the Earth's spin on its axis, which causes the daily cycle of day and night.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The movement of the Earth around the Sun, taking approximately 365¼ days to complete one cycle, is called
questions.explanation: Revolution refers to the Earth's annual orbit around the Sun, which, combined with axial tilt, produces the seasons.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The alternation of day and night is directly caused by the Earth's
questions.explanation: As the Earth rotates, different parts face the Sun (daytime) or away from it (nighttime), producing the day-night cycle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The changing seasons experienced at different times of the year are mainly caused by the
options: changing distance between the Earth and the Moon
tilt of the Earth's axis combined with its revolution around the Sun
Earth's rotation on its axis alone
changing speed of the Earth's rotation
questions.explanation: As the tilted Earth orbits the Sun, different hemispheres receive varying intensities of sunlight at different times of year, producing seasons.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The outermost, thin, solid layer of the Earth on which we live is called the
questions.explanation: The crust, part of the lithosphere, is the Earth's outermost solid layer, relatively thin compared to the layers beneath it.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The thick layer of the Earth found between the crust and the core, composed of hot, semi-solid rock, is called the
questions.explanation: The mantle lies beneath the crust and above the core, consisting of dense, hot rock that can flow slowly over long periods.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The innermost layer of the Earth, believed to consist mainly of iron and nickel, is called the
questions.explanation: The core, at the centre of the Earth, is composed largely of iron and nickel and is divided into a solid inner core and liquid outer core.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Rocks formed from the cooling and solidification of molten magma or lava are called
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks form directly from the cooling of magma (below ground) or lava (on the surface).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Rocks formed from the compaction and cementation of layers of sediment over long periods are called
questions.explanation: Sedimentary rocks form as layers of eroded material accumulate and are compressed and cemented together over time.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Rocks that have been changed in structure or mineral composition by intense heat and/or pressure are called
questions.explanation: Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are transformed by heat, pressure, or chemically active fluids, without fully melting.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The bending or buckling of rock layers due to compressional earth movements is called
questions.explanation: Folding occurs when horizontal compressional forces cause rock layers to bend, often producing mountain ranges.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A fracture in the Earth's crust along which rock masses have moved relative to one another is called a
questions.explanation: Faulting occurs when rock strata break and shift along a fracture line, often associated with earthquakes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Sudden, violent shaking of the ground caused by the release of energy along a fault line is called
questions.explanation: Earthquakes result from the sudden release of built-up stress along faults, generating seismic waves that shake the ground.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A sheet of igneous rock intruded parallel to existing rock layers underground is called a
questions.explanation: A sill is a horizontal (or near-horizontal) intrusion of magma that solidifies between existing rock layers.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A large, basin-shaped depression formed after a volcanic eruption or the collapse of a volcano's summit is called a
questions.explanation: A caldera is a broad depression resulting from the collapse of land following a major eruption or emptying of a magma chamber.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The breakdown of rocks in situ through the mechanical action of temperature changes, frost, or plant roots, without chemical change, is called
questions.explanation: Physical weathering breaks rock into smaller fragments through mechanical processes, without altering its chemical composition.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The breakdown or decomposition of rocks through chemical reactions such as oxidation and carbonation is called
questions.explanation: Chemical weathering alters the mineral composition of rocks through reactions with water, oxygen, and carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A rapid, sudden downward movement of a large mass of rock and soil down a slope is called a
questions.explanation: Landslides involve the fast, often catastrophic, movement of large volumes of material downslope, usually triggered by heavy rain or instability.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The stage of a river's course characterised by rapid vertical erosion, waterfalls, and V-shaped valleys is called the
questions.explanation: In its upper (youthful) course, a river actively cuts downward, producing steep-sided V-shaped valleys and features like waterfalls and rapids.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A loop-shaped lake formed when a meander is cut off from the main river channel is called an
questions.explanation: An oxbow lake forms when a river meander is bypassed and cut off, leaving a crescent-shaped body of standing water.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A landform created at a river's mouth where sediment is deposited as the river enters a sea or lake is called a
questions.explanation: A delta forms as a river loses velocity upon entering a larger body of water, depositing its sediment load in a fan-like or triangular shape.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Landforms produced when waves erode a coastline, such as cliffs and wave-cut platforms, result mainly from
questions.explanation: Coastal erosion, driven by wave action, sculpts features such as cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, and arches along shorelines.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Landforms such as sand dunes and yardangs, common in arid regions, are shaped mainly by
questions.explanation: In deserts, wind is a dominant agent of erosion and deposition, sculpting features like sand dunes through the movement of loose sediment.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The degree of hotness or coldness of the atmosphere, measured using a thermometer, is called
questions.explanation: Temperature measures the heat energy in the air and is a fundamental element of weather and climate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The force exerted by the weight of the atmosphere on the Earth's surface, measured using a barometer, is called
questions.explanation: Atmospheric pressure reflects the weight of the air above a given point, and its variations drive wind patterns.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The horizontal movement of air from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure is called
questions.explanation: Wind results from pressure differences in the atmosphere, with air flowing from high-pressure to low-pressure zones.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The amount of water vapour present in the air is called
questions.explanation: Humidity measures the moisture content of the air, which influences cloud formation and the likelihood of precipitation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Water falling from the atmosphere to the Earth's surface in forms such as rain, snow, and hail is called
questions.explanation: Precipitation includes all forms of moisture that fall from clouds to the ground, driven by condensation processes in the atmosphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The weather instrument used to measure atmospheric temperature is the
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures the temperature of the air, typically housed in a shaded, ventilated enclosure called a Stevenson screen.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The weather instrument used to measure atmospheric pressure is the
questions.explanation: A barometer measures the pressure exerted by the atmosphere, helping to forecast changes in weather.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The weather instrument used to measure wind speed is the
questions.explanation: An anemometer measures the speed of the wind, typically using rotating cups exposed to the airflow.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The instrument used to indicate wind direction is the
questions.explanation: A wind vane points in the direction from which the wind is blowing, showing wind direction rather than speed.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The instrument used to measure the amount of rainfall received at a location is the
questions.explanation: A rain gauge collects and measures the depth of rainfall over a set period at a particular location.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The instrument used to measure atmospheric humidity is the
questions.explanation: A hygrometer measures the amount of water vapour (relative humidity) present in the air.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Weather instruments are typically placed in a white, louvred box mounted on a stand, known as a
questions.explanation: A Stevenson screen shields instruments like thermometers from direct sunlight and precipitation while allowing free air circulation for accurate readings.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The hot, wet climate found near the equator, with high year-round temperatures and rainfall, is called the
questions.explanation: The equatorial climate is characterised by consistently high temperatures and abundant rainfall throughout the year, supporting dense rainforest vegetation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The hot, dry climate typically found in regions such as the Sahara, with very low and unreliable rainfall, is called the
questions.explanation: Hot desert climates experience extremely low rainfall and large diurnal temperature ranges, supporting sparse desert vegetation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A climatic zone experiencing moderate temperatures and rainfall spread across four distinct seasons is called a
questions.explanation: Temperate climates, found in the mid-latitudes, typically feature four seasons with moderate variations in temperature and precipitation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A very cold climatic zone found near the poles, with extremely low temperatures and minimal precipitation, is called a
questions.explanation: Polar climates are characterised by long, extremely cold winters and short, cool summers, with vegetation limited mainly to mosses and lichens.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The dense forest vegetation found in areas of the equatorial climate, characterised by tall trees and multiple canopy layers, is called
questions.explanation: Tropical rainforests thrive under the high rainfall and temperatures of equatorial regions, producing dense, multi-layered vegetation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The vegetation zone characterised by grassland interspersed with scattered trees, common across much of West Africa between the forest and desert, is called
questions.explanation: The savanna is a transitional vegetation belt of grasses and scattered trees, adapted to a climate with distinct wet and dry seasons.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The vegetation type typical of hot desert regions, adapted to survive with very little water, includes plants such as
questions.explanation: Desert vegetation consists mainly of xerophytes, plants specially adapted with features like thick stems and reduced leaves to conserve water.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The vegetation zone found in polar and sub-polar regions, consisting mainly of mosses, lichens, and low shrubs due to permanently frozen subsoil, is called the
questions.explanation: Tundra vegetation is limited by extreme cold and permafrost, supporting only low-growing plants adapted to short growing seasons.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A key factor influencing the distribution of vegetation across the world is
options: the number of rivers in a country
the size of a country's population
the colour of the local soil alone
climate, especially temperature and rainfall patterns
questions.explanation: Climate, particularly rainfall and temperature, is the primary control on which types of vegetation can grow in a given region.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The distinct layers of soil, visible when a vertical cut is made into the ground, are collectively called the
questions.explanation: A soil profile shows the sequence of layers (horizons) that make up the soil, from the surface down to the parent rock.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The uppermost, most fertile layer of soil, rich in organic matter (humus), is called
questions.explanation: Topsoil is the fertile surface layer where most plant roots and organic decomposition occur, making it critical for agriculture.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The removal of the fertile topsoil layer by the action of wind or water is called
questions.explanation: Soil erosion strips away valuable topsoil, reducing agricultural productivity and often caused by deforestation, overgrazing, or poor farming practices.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A common method used to reduce soil erosion on farmland with sloping terrain is
questions.explanation: Terracing and contour ploughing slow the flow of water down slopes, reducing the erosive power of surface runoff on farmland.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The general shape and features of the floor of the ocean, including ridges, trenches, and plains, is referred to as
questions.explanation: Ocean floor configuration describes the relief of the seabed, including features such as mid-ocean ridges, abyssal plains, and deep trenches.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Large-scale, persistent movements of ocean water in a fairly constant direction are called
questions.explanation: Ocean currents are continuous, directed movements of seawater, driven by factors such as wind, temperature, and salinity differences.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Ocean currents that carry warm water from tropical regions toward higher latitudes are called
questions.explanation: Warm currents originate near the equator and move warm water polewards, often raising coastal temperatures along their path.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Ocean currents that carry cold water from polar regions toward the tropics are called
questions.explanation: Cold currents flow from higher latitudes toward the equator, often cooling coastal climates and contributing to desert formation nearby.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Benguela Current, a cold ocean current flowing along the south-western coast of Africa, has the effect of
options: reducing rainfall and contributing to desert conditions along the adjacent coast
increasing rainfall and creating tropical rainforest along the coast
causing frequent volcanic eruptions along the coast
questions.explanation: Cold currents like the Benguela cool and stabilise the air above them, suppressing rainfall and helping to create arid coastal conditions, as seen near the Namib Desert.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The uneven distribution of the world's population, with dense clusters in some regions and sparse settlement in others, is best explained mainly by differences in
options: the exact shape of a country's borders
climate, relief, soil fertility, and economic opportunities
the number of rivers with no other factor
the length of a country's coastline alone
questions.explanation: Population distribution is shaped by a combination of physical factors (climate, relief, soils) and human/economic factors (job opportunities, infrastructure).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Regions with harsh climates, poor soils, or rugged relief, such as deserts and high mountains, typically have
options: a population density equal to fertile plains
the highest population density in the world
questions.explanation: Areas with challenging physical conditions for farming and settlement generally support fewer people, resulting in sparse population density.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Fertile river valleys and plains, such as the Nile Valley, typically have
questions.explanation: Fertile lowland areas with reliable water supply support intensive agriculture, attracting dense human settlement.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The movement of people from rural areas to urban centres in search of better economic opportunities is called
questions.explanation: Rural-urban migration describes the widespread movement of people from the countryside to cities and towns, often driven by the search for jobs and services.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A major factor commonly pushing people to migrate from rural to urban areas in West Africa is
options: limited job opportunities and poor social amenities in rural areas
an oversupply of social amenities in rural areas
the total absence of any cities to migrate to
questions.explanation: Rural areas often lack sufficient employment, healthcare, and educational facilities, pushing residents toward cities in search of a better life.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Settlements whose main economic activities are farming, fishing, and other primary occupations are generally classified as
questions.explanation: Rural settlements are typically characterised by low population density and reliance on primary economic activities such as agriculture.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Settlements characterised by high population density, and dominated by commerce, industry, and administrative functions, are generally classified as
questions.explanation: Urban settlements (towns and cities) are marked by dense populations and a concentration of secondary and tertiary economic activities.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The type of shifting agriculture in which farmers clear and cultivate land for a few years before moving on to allow the land to regenerate is called
questions.explanation: Shifting cultivation involves rotating farmland use, clearing new plots as older ones lose fertility, common in traditional tropical farming systems.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Farming carried out permanently on the same piece of land, often supported by fertilisers to maintain soil fertility, is called
questions.explanation: Sedentary farming involves continuous cultivation of a fixed plot of land, relying on soil management techniques rather than relocating.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Large-scale, organised farming of a single cash crop, such as rubber or oil palm, mainly for export, is called
questions.explanation: Plantation agriculture involves large, often monoculture farms producing cash crops for sale, typically requiring significant capital investment.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A system of livestock rearing in which herders move their animals from place to place in search of pasture and water is called
questions.explanation: Pastoral nomadism is common in semi-arid regions where herders must constantly relocate their livestock to find adequate grazing and water.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The exploitation of trees from natural or planted forests for timber and other wood products is called
questions.explanation: Lumbering involves the felling, processing, and marketing of timber, an important economic activity in forested regions of West Africa.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A major problem associated with lumbering in West Africa is
options: the complete absence of forest resources in the region
an oversupply of timber with no market demand
excessive government restriction preventing any logging
deforestation and loss of biodiversity from overexploitation
questions.explanation: Unsustainable logging practices in West Africa have contributed to significant deforestation, threatening biodiversity and forest-dependent livelihoods.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A key measure used to conserve forest resources exploited through lumbering is
options: clearing all forests for farmland immediately
banning all use of timber products permanently
questions.explanation: Sustainable forestry practices, such as replanting trees and limiting harvest rates, help conserve forest resources for future use.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Nigeria's most economically significant mineral resource, extracted mainly from the Niger Delta region, is
questions.explanation: Crude oil, concentrated in the Niger Delta, is Nigeria's most valuable mineral resource and dominant export earner.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A major coal mining town historically associated with Nigeria's coal industry is
questions.explanation: Enugu became a major centre of Nigeria's coal mining industry, which was historically significant before the rise of petroleum.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A prominent location for tin mining on the Jos Plateau in Nigeria is closely associated with the town of
questions.explanation: The Jos Plateau has long been associated with Nigeria's tin mining industry, alongside associated columbite deposits.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Iron ore deposits significant to Nigeria's steel industry are notably found around
questions.explanation: Itakpe in Kogi State hosts major iron ore deposits, feeding Nigeria's steel production efforts, including the Ajaokuta Steel Complex.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Bauxite, an ore used mainly in the production of aluminium, is significant in some West African countries, most notably
questions.explanation: Guinea holds some of the world's largest bauxite reserves, making it a major global supplier of this aluminium ore.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Gold mining has long been economically significant in parts of West Africa, particularly in
questions.explanation: Ghana, historically known as the 'Gold Coast', has a long tradition of gold mining that remains economically important today.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The location of industries close to their sources of raw materials, markets, or labour supply is influenced mainly by
options: industrial location factors such as proximity to raw materials, markets, transport, and power supply
the colour of a country's flag
the length of a country's history
the number of political parties in a country
questions.explanation: Industries typically locate where costs are minimised and access to inputs, markets, and infrastructure is most favourable.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A major challenge facing manufacturing industries in many developing West African countries is
options: inadequate infrastructure, such as unreliable power supply and poor transport networks
an oversupply of skilled labour with no jobs available
too much government investment in industry
questions.explanation: Poor infrastructure, especially unreliable electricity and transport, significantly raises production costs and limits industrial growth in the region.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The mode of transport generally considered most flexible for door-to-door movement of goods and people over short to medium distances is
questions.explanation: Road transport offers the greatest flexibility, reaching destinations that other transport modes, such as rail or water, cannot access directly.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The mode of transport generally most economical for moving heavy, bulky goods over long distances within a country is
options: road transport for very long hauls
questions.explanation: Rail transport can move large volumes of heavy freight efficiently over long overland distances, often more cheaply than road transport.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The mode of transport most suitable for moving goods and passengers between countries separated by large bodies of water is
questions.explanation: Sea transport remains the dominant means of moving bulky goods internationally, especially between countries separated by oceans.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: West Africa's physical setting is generally characterised by
options: the complete absence of any river systems
a landscape consisting entirely of high fold mountains
a continuous ice sheet covering the entire region
a mix of coastal plains, plateaus, and river basins such as the Niger and Senegal basins
questions.explanation: West Africa's relief includes coastal lowlands, extensive plateaus, and major river systems like the Niger, shaping its human and economic geography.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The River Niger, one of West Africa's most important rivers, generally flows through countries including
questions.explanation: The Niger River originates in Guinea and flows through Mali, Niger, and Nigeria before emptying into the Gulf of Guinea via its delta.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A major environmental challenge facing the Sahel region on the edge of the Sahara Desert is
options: excessive year-round rainfall causing constant flooding
permanent snow cover across the region
desertification, caused by overgrazing, deforestation, and low rainfall
an overabundance of forest cover with no farmland
questions.explanation: The Sahel faces desertification as unsustainable land use combines with low and unreliable rainfall, gradually turning productive land into desert.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A significant environmental problem in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria, linked to petroleum extraction, is
options: oil pollution affecting land, water, and local livelihoods
a complete absence of any industrial activity
questions.explanation: Oil spills and gas flaring associated with petroleum extraction in the Niger Delta have caused significant environmental damage, harming farming and fishing livelihoods.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Regional cooperation among West African states, particularly through bodies such as ECOWAS, is aimed mainly at
options: encouraging countries to withdraw from all international cooperation
restricting all trade and movement between member countries
eliminating the need for any national governments
promoting economic integration, free trade, and regional stability
questions.explanation: Regional bodies like ECOWAS seek to foster cooperation on trade, security, and development among West African nations.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Coastal flooding is an increasing environmental challenge for many West African cities mainly because of
options: a combination of rising sea levels, heavy rainfall, and poor urban drainage systems
a permanent decrease in regional rainfall
the complete absence of any coastline in the region
questions.explanation: Coastal West African cities face growing flood risk due to a mix of climatic factors, such as heavy rains and rising seas, combined with inadequate drainage infrastructure.
